prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: the trapping of many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength and its development to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B001) with Katori and Ye as my single-part configuration; my preferred configuration has not changed since round 1. The chair asks what is new relative to 2005 and 2012. The frequency comb gave a way to count optical cycles, and the single-ion work gave control of one quantum system. Neither addressed the central limit of ion clocks, which is the statistical power of a single absorber. The lattice clock removes that limit by interrogating thousands of neutral atoms in a trap whose light shift cancels on the clock transition at the magic wavelength, while the atoms stay confined in the Lamb-Dicke regime. That is a different design principle, and it moved fractional uncertainty from the 1e-16 range to 1e-18 and opened a regime where many-body interactions and collective coherence matter. A citation that names the magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms states this distinction without crediting the comb or ion-clock lines, and it does not imply credit to the other lattice-clock groups. The two-name credit is clean, the performance is reproduced in several national laboratories and compared across continents, and the consequences in constants tests, geodesy and dark-matter searches are already realised. None of this depends on the formal redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and a third prize in optical frequency metrology in about twenty-five years is a fair objection that I cannot dismiss as a mere perception. Credit is also not perfectly sharp: Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and Paris groups contributed to early lattice-clock work, and a two-name prize necessarily leaves them outside. On the chair's request for priority chronology, I have not checked the primary papers in this exchange, and I am relying on my general knowledge that the magic-wavelength proposal and the first neutral-atom lattice-clock demonstrations are associated with Katori's group and that Ye's group led the later accuracy records. I would not claim that chronology is verified. Finally, B013 is a more novel discovery and I cannot show that the conceptual step of the clock is larger.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B013 first, argues that the open pairing mechanism should not weigh heavily because the citation rests on flat bands and the correlated phases, and says that B001 is the safer pick if maturity is weighted over novelty.
responses.response: I accept your argument that a citation can be written without the pairing mechanism, and that removes part of my round-1 objection. What remains is twist-angle disorder and device-to-device variability, which you also mention, and that these bear on how secure the phase diagram is as an established result after about eight years. I also do not agree that the conceptual step of the clock is small. The step from one ion to thousands of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength changes the statistical and systematic regime, and I would say that is a new principle in measurement, not only a refinement. I agree with you that if the committee weighs maturity and clean credit, B001 is the safer choice, and that is the way I weigh them.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the prediction-to-confirmation chain for twisted bilayer graphene is already long, that the correlated insulators and superconducting domes are reproduced across platforms, and that Andrei's exclusion should be stated openly, not hidden.
responses.response: Your reply moved me on one point: reproduction across laboratories and across moire platforms is stronger than I credited in round 1, and I now treat B013 as a serious near-term candidate, which is why it stays first among my alternatives. I have not moved on the attribution question. You say that Andrei's STM work preceded the magic-angle prediction and did not discover the correlated phases, and I follow that. But the committee would still be explaining in public why a three-person cap excludes an early, real experimental claim, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is not separable. For the clock prize the corresponding exclusions are of groups that came after the proposal and the first demonstrations, which I find easier to state. I would still ask you whether you would support B013 if the citation stated the Andrei exclusion in the committee record.

responses.point: Olsson moved from B013 first in the opening to B001, noting that she trades some originality for cleaner attribution and maturity, and relies on general knowledge for the credit among Ido, Takamoto, Lemonde and the NIST and PTB teams.
responses.response: I would not describe your trade as a loss of originality, since the clock introduces a new principle and not only a better instrument, but I understand why you flag it. On the unverified chronology, I am in the same position as you and have said so above. What I can add as a theorist who works with microwave quantum optics is that the discriminating physical point is state-insensitive confinement, which the magic-wavelength condition provides, and that point attaches to the proposal and first realisation and not to later groups that adopted it. That is the best reason I have to think the line around Katori and Ye is defensible, though it is not a substitute for checking the primary papers before any final decision. I also note your Chalmers connection to me, which does not affect my view on B001.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B001 for its broad support and clean attribution, while noting that a committee preferring new quantum matter to precision measurement could reasonably choose B013 or B024.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning on attribution and maturity, and I want to be explicit that I do not count the eight-member ranking as a reason in itself. The scientific arguments carry it. On your remark about new quantum matter, the lattice clock also has a many-body side, because Ye's group showed spin-exchange and collective effects at the 1e-18 level, so it is not purely a metrology result. I still regard B024 as the next strongest case on science, and I have not changed my view that its three-name cut is harder to defend than the clock credit, because Hasan's 3D work and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction fall outside Kane, Mele and Molenkamp.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, in particular a third optical frequency metrology prize in about twenty-five years.
The priority chronology for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice-clock demonstrations, which I have not verified from primary sources.
Whether B013 will be judged mature enough, given the open pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder, and whether the Andrei exclusion can be defended in a public statement.
Whether B024 can be given a defensible three-name scope given Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. Circuit QED (B029) falls squarely within my own research and my role as director of WACQT at Chalmers, where Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson are colleagues, Anton Frisk Kockum is a frequent co-author, and several researchers associated with the 2025 prize have visited; I recuse myself from any decision on B029 and I do not place it in my configuration or alternatives. Eva Olsson is a Chalmers colleague, which I regard as collegial and not specific to B001. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B013 or B024.
